passages.title: Duchess
passages.intro: Read the story below, then answer questions 1–6. Paragraphs are numbered.
passages.credit: Original story written for this practice test.
paragraphs: Nobody in the Tran family could remember who had named the chook Duchess, but everyone agreed the name suited her. She walked around the backyard as if she owned it, and she looked at people the way a queen looks at a puddle.
Every morning, Minh's job was to collect the eggs. Every morning, Duchess sat on them and refused to move.
'Just lift her up,' said his sister Lan, who was sixteen and had an answer for everything.
Minh had tried that. Duchess had pecked him so hard on the thumb that he had yelped loud enough to set off the neighbour's dog.

On Saturday, Minh tried something new. He sat down on an upturned bucket outside the coop and began to read his library book out loud. It was about a girl who sailed around the world, and it had a lot of storms in it. Minh read the stormy parts in a big, dramatic voice.
After a while, Duchess put her head on one side. After a longer while, she stood up, stretched one leg, and stepped down from the nest to listen more closely.
Minh slipped his hand into the nest. Three eggs, still warm.

He read to Duchess every morning after that. By the end of the month they had sailed around the world twice, and Lan had started finding reasons to hang around the back door, pretending not to listen.

passages.title: The Red Crab March
passages.intro: Read the text below. Choose the best word to fill each of the 8 gaps (questions 7–14).
passages.credit: Original text written for this practice test.
passages.text:
Every year, thousands of red crabs on Christmas Island {1} an amazing journey. When the first rains of the wet season arrive, the crabs leave the forest and {2} towards the sea. They cross roads, gardens and even golf courses on the {3}.

To keep the crabs safe, the people who live on the island close some roads and build special bridges for the crabs to {4} over. Signs warn drivers to {5} down.

At the beach, each female crab lays her eggs in the water. A few weeks {6}, millions of tiny baby crabs come out of the sea and march back to the forest. It is one of the most {7} sights in the natural world, and visitors come from all {8} the globe to see it.

passages.title: Mulga Bill's Bicycle
passages.intro: Read the poem below, then answer questions 15–19. Lines are numbered. (resplendent: dazzling; blows: boasts; abode: home; fray: battle; ere: before; narrer shaves: narrow escapes; give best: admit defeat.)
passages.credit: A. B. ('Banjo') Paterson, first published in the Sydney Mail, 1896. Public domain.
stanzas: 'Twas Mulga Bill, from Eaglehawk, that caught the cycling craze;
He turned away the good old horse that served him many days;
He dressed himself in cycling clothes, resplendent to be seen;
He hurried off to town and bought a shining new machine;
And as he wheeled it through the door, with air of lordly pride,
The grinning shop assistant said, 'Excuse me, can you ride?'
'See, here, young man,' said Mulga Bill, 'from Walgett to the sea,
From Conroy's Gap to Castlereagh, there's none can ride like me.
I'm good all round at everything, as everybody knows,
Although I'm not the one to talk – I hate a man that blows.
But riding is my special gift, my chiefest, sole delight;
Just ask a wild duck can it swim, a wild cat can it fight.
There's nothing clothed in hair or hide, or built of flesh or steel,
There's nothing walks or jumps, or runs, on axle, hoof, or wheel,
But what I'll sit, while hide will hold and girths and straps are tight:
I'll ride this here two-wheeled concern right straight away at sight.'
'Twas Mulga Bill, from Eaglehawk, that sought his own abode,
That perched above the Dead Man's Creek, beside the mountain road.
He turned the cycle down the hill and mounted for the fray,
But ere he'd gone a dozen yards it bolted clean away.
It left the track, and through the trees, just like a silver streak,
It whistled down the awful slope, towards the Dead Man's Creek.
It shaved a stump by half an inch, it dodged a big white-box:
The very wallaroos in fright went scrambling up the rocks,
The wombats hiding in their caves dug deeper underground,
As Mulga Bill, as white as chalk, sat tight to every bound.
It struck a stone and gave a spring that cleared a fallen tree,
It raced beside a precipice as close as close could be;
And then as Mulga Bill let out one last despairing shriek
It made a leap of twenty feet into the Dead Man's Creek.
'Twas Mulga Bill, from Eaglehawk, that slowly swam ashore:
He said, 'I've had some narrer shaves and lively rides before;
I've rode a wild bull round a yard to win a five pound bet,
But this was the most awful ride that I've encountered yet.
I'll give that two-wheeled outlaw best; it's shaken all my nerve
To feel it whistle through the air and plunge and buck and swerve.
It's safe at rest in Dead Man's Creek, we'll leave it lying still;
A horse's back is good enough henceforth for Mulga Bill.'

passages.title: Not Really a Nut
passages.intro: Six sentences have been removed from the article. Choose the sentence (A–G) that best fits each gap (questions 20–25). There is one extra sentence you do not need.
passages.credit: Original article written for this practice test.
paragraphs: If you have ever eaten a peanut butter sandwich, you might think peanuts are nuts. [[1]] They grow underground, in the roots of a plant, which makes them more like peas and beans.
The peanut plant is small and bushy, with yellow flowers. [[2]] It bends down towards the soil and pushes itself into the ground. There, under the dirt, the peanut pods grow.
Farmers dig up the whole plant when the peanuts are ready. [[3]] After a few days in the sun, the peanuts are dry enough to be taken off the plants.
[[4]] In Australia, most of them are grown in Queensland, where the weather is warm. Some are roasted and salted, while others are crushed to make oil.
Many people make the peanuts into peanut butter. [[5]] Then the crushed peanuts are mixed with a little salt and oil until they are smooth.
Peanuts are full of goodness, but some people are allergic to them. [[6]] That is why many schools ask families not to send peanuts in lunchboxes.

bank.A: They leave the plants lying in the field so the peanuts can dry out.
bank.B: In fact, they are not nuts at all.
bank.C: The peanuts are roasted first and then crushed in a machine.
bank.D: After a flower dies, a little stalk grows from it.
bank.E: Even a tiny amount can make them very sick.
bank.F: Peanuts are grown in many countries around the world.
bank.G: Some birds love to eat sunflower seeds.

passages.title: Four Short Texts
passages.intro: Read the four short texts. For questions 26–33, choose which text (A, B, C or D) each statement matches. You can use each letter more than once.
passages.credit: Original texts written for this practice test.

A.title: The Library Cat
A.text: Our town library has a cat called Biscuit. She arrived one rainy night eight years ago and never left. Biscuit sleeps in the picture-book box and likes to sit on the newspapers when people are trying to read them. Some visitors come just to see her. The librarians say she is the best worker they have, because she makes everyone smile and never asks for a pay rise.

B.title: A Letter to the Council
B.text: Dear Councillors, I am writing about the playground in Banksia Park. The slide is cracked and the swings squeak so loudly that the birds fly away. My little brother cut his hand on a broken bolt last week. Please fix the playground before somebody is badly hurt. Many children use it every day, and we would look after it if it were safe. Yours sincerely, Ellie (aged 9)

C.title: How to Grow a Bean in a Jar
C.text: You will need a glass jar, some paper towel, water and a dried bean. Fold the paper towel and push it around the inside of the jar. Slide the bean between the paper and the glass, so you can see it. Add a little water to keep the paper damp, but not soaking. Put the jar somewhere bright. In a few days, a root will grow down, and then a shoot will push up towards the light.

D.title: My Grandad's Tractor
D.text: My grandad's tractor is older than my dad. It is red, or it used to be, and it coughs like an old man when it starts. Grandad won't sell it, even though he has a new one. He says it ploughed every paddock on the farm and carried my dad home from school when the creek flooded. Sometimes I see him sitting on it in the shed, just thinking.

questions.stem: Duchess looked at people 'the way a queen looks at a puddle' (paragraph 1). This means she

options.B: liked to look at her reflection.
options.C: thought she was much more important than everyone else.

questions.explanation: A queen would look down on a puddle as something unimportant. Duchess acts as if she is far more important than the people around her.

distractors.A: the puddle is part of the comparison; it's not about being scared
distractors.B: nothing mentions reflections
distractors.D: the comparison is about her attitude, not her looks

questions.stem: What does paragraph 3 suggest about Lan?

options.A: She often gives advice, even when she doesn't really know.
options.B: She is good at looking after chooks.
options.C: She wants to collect the eggs herself.

questions.explanation: Lan 'had an answer for everything', and her answer here (just lift her up) doesn't work, as Minh already knows. The writer is gently teasing her.

distractors.B: her advice doesn't work, so she isn't shown to be good with chooks
distractors.C: nothing suggests she wants the job
distractors.D: she tells Minh to lift Duchess, so she doesn't seem scared

questions.stem: Why does the writer include the detail about the neighbour's dog (paragraph 4)?

options.A: to show that the neighbour's dog is dangerous
options.B: to explain why Minh doesn't like dogs
options.C: to show that Duchess is afraid of dogs
options.D: to show how much the peck hurt Minh

questions.explanation: Minh yelped so loudly that it set off the dog next door. This funny detail shows how hard Duchess pecked.

distractors.A: the dog only barks; it isn't shown as dangerous
distractors.B: nothing is said about Minh's feelings about dogs
distractors.C: Duchess's reaction to the dog isn't mentioned

questions.stem: Why does Minh's new idea work?

options.A: Duchess was hungry and wanted food.
options.B: Duchess became so interested in the story that she left the nest to listen.
options.C: The loud voice frightened Duchess off the nest.

questions.explanation: Duchess tilts her head, then steps down 'to listen more closely'. She is curious about the story, which gives Minh his chance.

distractors.A: food is never mentioned
distractors.C: she moves closer to listen, so she isn't frightened
distractors.D: Lan isn't there in this part

questions.stem: 'By the end of the month they had sailed around the world twice' (paragraph 8). What does this mean?

options.A: Minh and Duchess went on a long holiday.
options.B: Minh had read the whole book to Duchess two times.
options.C: Minh's family moved to another country.
options.D: Minh dreamed about sailing every night.

questions.explanation: The book is about a girl sailing around the world. 'Sailing around the world twice' is a playful way of saying Minh read the book to Duchess twice.

distractors.A: took the words literally
distractors.C: nothing about moving
distractors.D: nothing about dreams

questions.skill: Reading between the lines at the end
questions.stem: What does the last sentence suggest about Lan?

options.A: She is annoyed that Minh is wasting time.
options.B: She wants to borrow Minh's library book.
options.C: She is enjoying the story too, but doesn't want to admit it.
options.D: She is checking that Minh does his job.

questions.explanation: Lan 'started finding reasons to hang around' and pretends not to listen. Secretly, she is enjoying the story as much as Duchess is.

distractors.A: if she were annoyed, she wouldn't stay to listen
distractors.B: nothing says she wants to borrow it
distractors.D: she is pretending not to listen, not checking on him

options.B: He is pleased because he is Mulga Bill's friend.
options.C: He wants to borrow the bicycle.

questions.stem: In line 10, Mulga Bill says 'I'm not the one to talk – I hate a man that blows.' Why is this funny?

options.A: He hates people who play wind instruments.
options.C: He is boasting at the very moment he says he hates boasting.
options.D: He is too shy to talk to the shop assistant.

questions.explanation: 'Blows' means boasts. Bill says he hates show-offs, yet the whole stanza is him boasting that nobody can ride like him.

distractors.B: took 'blows' to mean the wind
distractors.D: he talks a lot, so he isn't shy

questions.stem: The bicycle goes down the hill 'just like a silver streak' (line 21). This suggests that it

options.A: is very shiny and moving extremely fast.
options.C: is leaving a trail of paint.

questions.explanation: A streak is a quick line of light or colour. The shiny new bike flashes past so fast that it looks like a silver streak.

distractors.B: the comparison is about how it looks, not what it is made of
distractors.C: took 'streak' too literally
distractors.D: it 'bolted clean away': it was fast

questions.stem: Why does the poet say the wombats 'dug deeper underground' (line 25)?

options.A: to show that wombats are good at digging
options.B: to explain why there are holes on the hill
options.C: to show that it was a very hot day
options.D: to exaggerate how frightening and wild the ride is

questions.explanation: Even animals hiding underground are pretending to be scared. This funny exaggeration shows how wild the ride is.

distractors.A: true, but not why the poet includes it
distractors.B: the holes aren't the point
distractors.C: nothing about the weather

questions.stem: What has Mulga Bill decided at the end of the poem?

options.A: He will buy a better bicycle.
options.B: He will learn to swim properly.
options.C: He will go back to riding horses.
options.D: He will try to ride a wild bull.

questions.explanation: He leaves the bike 'at rest in Dead Man's Creek' and says 'A horse's back is good enough henceforth' (from now on) for him.

distractors.A: he leaves the bike in the creek and gives up cycling
distractors.B: he swims ashore, but swimming isn't his decision
distractors.D: he mentions riding a wild bull in the past
